title: Two-thirds
primary_topics: Escudero's ruling that 16 of 24 votes are needed to convict VP Sara Duterte regardless of senators detained, in hiding, sick or absent -- a literal reading of Art. XI's 'two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate'
How the Supreme Court sets its majority -- Internal Rules: quorum of eight en banc, decision by majority of members who actually took part; the denominator shifts with ACTIVE participation

Examples -- League of Cities v. Comelec flip-flops (6-5, 6-4 with denominator 10, 7-6 with 13); Cruz v. DENR Secretary 7-7 deadlock upholding IPRA; De Castro v. JBC on deliberation as the core of decision-making
Limits of the analogy -- the SC reviews questions of law and is not a trier of facts, while the impeachment court receives evidence and hears witnesses
Thesis -- the Senate need not blindly follow the Court's method, but the two-thirds rule cannot be applied without first identifying the correct denominator

Escudero's ruling is interlocutory and 'not written in stone' -- reversible by simple majority; the SC will intervene only for grave abuse of discretion, anchoring the power to the rule of law against partisan passion

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban examines Senate presiding officer Francis 'Chiz' Escudero's ruling that 16 of 24 votes are needed to convict VP Sara Duterte, regardless of senators who are detained, hiding, sick or otherwise unable to participate -- a literal reading of the Constitution's 'two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate.' Not a politician, CJP offers a judicial perspective on how the Supreme Court sets its voting denominator. Under its Internal Rules, the Court needs a quorum of eight en banc, and a decision requires the majority of members who actually took part; the denominator shifts with active participation. In League of Cities v. Comelec, the Court struck down the Cityhood Laws 6-5 in 2008, upheld them 6-4 in 2009 when vacancies and abstentions cut the denominator to 10, then reinstated its first ruling 7-6 with 13. In Cruz v. DENR Secretary, a 14-member Court deadlocked 7-7, so the challenge to the Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act failed. In De Castro v. JBC, the Court stressed that deliberation is the core of decision-making and that one voice less is a contributed opinion less. Yet these examples do not settle the question: the SC reviews questions of law and is not a trier of facts, while the impeachment court receives evidence and hears witnesses. CJP does not ask the Senate to copy the Court, but argues that the two-thirds requirement cannot be applied without first identifying the correct denominator. Escudero's ruling is interlocutory, not written in stone, and may be reversed by a simple majority. The Court will intervene only for grave abuse of discretion; since the impeachment court is susceptible to shifting public moods, the SC's duty, when petitioned, is to anchor its power to the rule of law rather than partisan passion.
